title: Selected Aspects of Diagnosis and Therapy in Dissociative Identity Disorder (DID)—Case Report
case_prompt:
A 33-year-old woman presented for evaluation of episodic changes in her behavior and memory. Since 2014, she described hearing a “voice in her head” that she attributed to different identities or “alters,” especially during stressful situations when these alters urged her toward self-harm. She works full-time as a technical machine controller but experiences alternating periods of work incapacity and hyperproductivity, which colleagues have observed and linked to her switching states. 

Her psychiatric history includes a prior diagnosis of schizophrenia, treated briefly with olanzapine 5 mg daily and valproic acid 1000 mg daily; she discontinued treatment, feeling misunderstood. She sought a second opinion after reading about multiple personalities. She has a history of self-injury with a razor blade and one suicide attempt by hanging. 

Her family background is notable for a conflictual parental marriage; her mother had borderline personality disorder and died three years ago, and her father is critical and threatening. She reports nonconsensual advances during a college relationship and memory gaps in a later partnership. 

On mental-status examination, she was fully oriented, maintained variable eye contact, and spoke in a sensible but digressive manner. There were fluctuating mood and psychomotor drive corresponding with identity switches. She denied delusions, hallucinations, or current suicidal ideation. 

Routine laboratory studies, ECG, brain MRI, and EEG were all within normal limits.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Schizophrenia was excluded — “schizophrenia was ruled out during hospitalization, as the patient did not meet the diagnostic criteria.”  
2. Epilepsy was excluded — “she was diagnosed at the Neurology Outpatient Clinic due to a single episode of dissociative seizures; epilepsy was ruled out.”  
3. Borderline personality disorder was considered — “the data collected suggested the presence of a mixed cluster B personality disorder—histrionic, emotionally unstable, narcissistic, and antisocial personality traits.”  
4. Dissociative subtype of PTSD was considered and distinguished — “the diagnostic key feature of DID is episodes of mental blankness associated with switching between different identity states, which is not included in the diagnostic criteria for PTSD.”  
5. Symptom exaggeration (malingering) was considered — “the MMPI-2 profile suggested symptom amplification; however, further analysis took into account dissociative tendencies rather than deliberate symptom exaggeration.”
